note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Everything below comes from the City of Vancouver's own pickleball page and, for one address, from the City's park page that corroborates it. This is a small set — three venues — and it is small because the City lists a fourth without a court count and with an address that its own park page contradicts. Publishing three and explaining the fourth is the honest shape of what Vancouver has written down.

slots.parking: Not published, at any of the three. The City gives an address, a court count and, at Oakbrook, opening hours and a maintenance phone number, and says nothing anywhere about where to leave a car. Two of the three are community centres with their own car parks, which is a reasonable inference and not a verified fact, so it is not recorded as one. Oakbrook Community Park sits just west of I-205 in a residential neighbourhood; what that means for parking on a summer evening is exactly the kind of thing this directory will not guess at. If you are driving somewhere here for the first time, treat parking as unknown rather than assuming a lot.
slots.peak_hours: Vancouver publishes no hourly demand figures, but Firstenburg Community Center's rules describe a busy room in more detail than most cities manage about anything. Players must sign in on a sheet at the front desk, in person and only for themselves; sign-in opens at 6 a.m. for morning pickleball, at noon for the afternoon, and thirty minutes before every other session. Wristbands are issued at sign-in and must be worn to be on court. Once the maximum number of players has signed in, the session is marked FULL, and anyone arriving after that can pay the drop-in fee to join a waitlist that does not guarantee a game. A parks department does not write four paragraphs of queue management for a room nobody is fighting to get into. Outdoor, the City asks players to rotate in using a paddle rack and notes that scheduling apps do not reserve court time.
slots.surface_condition: One surface is stated in the whole city: Firstenburg's six courts are on a wood gymnasium floor. Oakbrook and Marshall say nothing about what they are made of, and neither reads as a category word we would have refused — the City simply does not mention it. On condition, Vancouver does something no other operator in this directory does: it publishes a route for reporting a broken court. Both outdoor sites carry a maintenance line, 360-487-8177, and a link to the Public Works request form for Grounds service. That is not a statement about the state of the courts, and we have not recorded it as one. It is a statement that somebody is responsible for them, which is worth more than a resurfacing date nobody updates.
slots.local_scene: Two things stand out. The first is that Vancouver's pickleball is organised around its community centres rather than its parks: the adult leagues for ages 14 and up and the youth league for ages 10 to 14 all play at Firstenburg, and clinics run at both Firstenburg and Marshall. The second is the Columbia River Pickleball Club, which the City names in an unusually practical way — at Fisher Basin Community Park, where nets are not provided, club members can reach club nets using a lockbox code. A city page that tells you which cupboard the nets are in is a city page written by someone who plays. Oakbrook is the counterpoint: four courts with nets and poles permanently installed, so nothing needs organising at all. Vancouver also warns, sensibly, that apps like PlayTime Scheduler and Pickleheads help players find each other but do not reserve court time on its courts.

best_for.heading: Best if you want to turn up and play outdoors
best_for.text: Oakbrook Community Park is the only outdoor pickleball in this set and it asks nothing of you: four dedicated courts, nets and poles permanently installed, open play for all skill levels, 7 a.m. to 10 p.m. daily, no reservations taken or possible. Bring a paddle. The one caveat is in the City's own words — the courts do not have lighting — so those 10 p.m. hours are theoretical for much of a Pacific Northwest year.

best_for.heading: Best if you want the most courts under a roof
best_for.text: Firstenburg Community Center has six courts on a wood gymnasium floor, the largest pickleball room in the city and the home of every one of Vancouver's leagues. Play is free if you are a member of the community centre and costs a daily drop-in fee if you are not — the City states that the fee exists and never states what it is, so we have not printed a number. Sessions run Monday to Friday for ages 12 and up and they do fill.

best_for.heading: Best if you are up before work
best_for.text: Marshall Community Center runs four indoor courts, and in high summer it runs them early: from 22 June to 22 August its pickleball hours move to 6 to 7:45 a.m., which the City explains is to keep dedicated court time without colliding with summer programming, in a cooler gym. It is a smaller room than Firstenburg and the same membership-or-drop-in arrangement applies.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Vancouver have?
faqs.a: We have verified 14 across three City of Vancouver venues: four outdoor at Oakbrook Community Park, six indoor at Firstenburg Community Center and four indoor at Marshall Community Center. The City lists a fourth site, Fisher Basin Community Park, without a court count — so it is not on this page, and the reasons are set out below rather than left as a silence.

faqs.q: Why is Fisher Basin Community Park not listed here?
faqs.a: Three reasons, any one of which would be enough. The City states no court count for it, only that it has shared tennis and pickleball courts. Its address on the pickleball page is 3103 NE 99th Ave — which is Oakbrook Community Park's address, printed two paragraphs above — while the City's own park page for Fisher Basin gives SE 192nd Ave, Vancouver, WA 98607, in a different part of the city with a different postcode. And no published address for it carries a house number, so the Census geocoder returns no match and we could not confirm where it is even if a count appeared. When a source contradicts itself, the answer is to say so, not to pick the half you prefer.

faqs.q: Do any Vancouver courts have lights?
faqs.a: No, and the City says so rather than leaving it blank. It writes that Oakbrook's courts "do not have lighting", which is a stated negative, so Oakbrook reads No. Firstenburg and Marshall are indoor rooms where the question does not arise and the City says nothing, so both read "not verified yet". Seattle's parks dataset answers the same question for twenty-four venues, five of which are lit and nineteen of which are not, so a No here is not unusual in this directory — what is unusual is that Vancouver answered it in a sentence rather than a field.

At Oakbrook, we do not know. It is a City park with open-play courts that cannot be reserved, and it is very probably free — but the City never uses the word, so we have not printed it. That is not pedantry: Portland is in this directory with a verified free because Portland wrote it down, and the difference between the two cities is the difference between a fact and an assumption. At Firstenburg and Marshall, play is free for community centre members and visitors pay a daily drop-in fee whose amount the City does not publish.

faqs.q: Do I need to bring a net?
faqs.a: Not at Oakbrook — nets and poles are permanently installed there, which is a rarer thing than it sounds. At Fisher Basin, which we do not publish, the City says nets are not provided and that Columbia River Pickleball Club members can get club nets from a lockbox. For the indoor centres the question is handled by the session rather than by you.

You sign in on the sheet by the front desk, in person, for yourself only. Sign-in opens at 6 a.m. for morning play, noon for the afternoon and thirty minutes before any other session. You are given a wristband and must wear it to be on court. Once the session hits its maximum it is FULL, and later arrivals can pay the drop-in fee to put a paddle on the waitlist without any guarantee of a game. On court, paddles queue on the bottom bench, courts are split competitive on the right and recreational on the left, and teams play two games and rotate out.

faqs.q: Is this Vancouver, Washington or Vancouver, Canada?
faqs.a: Washington. This is Vancouver in Clark County, Washington, on the north bank of the Columbia River directly across from Portland, Oregon — not Vancouver, British Columbia, which is about three hundred miles further north and in another country. Portland's own eleven pickleball venues are a few miles away over the bridge and are published on this site too.

faqs.q: What do you not know about these venues?
faqs.a: Parking, at all three — never mentioned. Surface at two of the three; only Firstenburg's wood floor is stated. The amount of the drop-in fee at both community centres. Restrooms at all three, including Oakbrook, whose park page lists one among its features but not in a form our committed snapshot preserves, so it is left unverified rather than published from something we cannot re-read.
